title: B2-18 · Talk shows and debates: the passive Levantine

blocks.text: B2-18 · Talk shows and debates: the passive Levantine
Lesson overview

Lebanese talk shows are among the most followed in the Arab world, and the Levantine (Lebanese, Syrian, Palestinian, Jordanian) is, after the Egyptian, the dialect that feels most in the media. You don't have to learn to speak: you have to understand it enough to follow a debate, recognize positions and report them. The good news is that you already know the fuṣḥā and the Egyptian: the Levantine is close to both, and with a dozen grammatical words, some pronunciation rules and formulas typical of the debate you can understand much more than you think. In this unity learn the main traits of the Levant (sounds, pronouns, verbs, negation, interrogative words), the lexicon of the debate (breaking, granting, rejecting) and a method to follow a discussion in which everyone speaks together. Three weeks, while the Moroccan track begins (MAG-01).

rows: B2 · Module B2.4 Variation and production

blocks.text: Materials This unit, Reference Grammar (G)77), talk show authentic levantini chosen by the tutor, a Levant speaker for scripts, sessions with the tutor
Targets. At the end of the lesson you know:
1. recognize the Levantine and distinguish it from the Egyptian and the fuṣḥā;
2. understand the main traits: pronunciation, pronouns and suffixes, present with b- and ʿam, future with raḥ, denial, interrogative words;
3. follow a Levant television debate, identifying who claims what and with what arguments and figures;
4. understand the formulas of the debate: interrupt, ask for the floor, grant, reject, thank;
5. report in fuṣḥā, neutrally, a debate heard in Levantine.
Three-week plan.

5. Pronunciation

Train your ear. Listen to the Guided Listening Dialog (Script B) and mark on a copy of the text: a) every ʾ which corresponds to one q of the fuṣḥā (ʾānūn, ʾurūḍ, šuʾaʾ); b) every ž (žadīd, yitžawwazu); c) the finals in -e (the- madīne, il-layle, sakaniyye); d) the suffixes -o, -kon, -on. Then listen back with your eyes closed and count how many times you hear ʿam and raḥ. You don't have to imitate these sounds: you have to recognize them.

7. Following a debate: the method

rows: read the title of the bet and the names and roles of the guests; predict positions (who defends, who criticizes)
follow the three questions of Sāra: who is with whom, who is against whom, what figures; write down keywords and numbers, not phrases
When they all speak together, listen to the moderator: repeat and summarize (yaʿni inta ʿam tʾūl Hymn...)
reconstruct for each guest: position, two arguments, one digit, one concession

blocks.text: after refer to fuṣḥā with attribution verbs (B2-08) and without taking a position

Neutral synthesis. To refer to a debate means to give each side the same space, with neutral verbs ( ⁧قال، رأى، أكد، اعتبر⁩ ) and without evaluation adjectives (B2-11). If a guest has raised his voice or interrupted, it can only be said if it is relevant and with neutral words ( ⁧قاطع، احتج⁩ ).
